extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, graduate students, and scholarly readers interested in cultural history of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological principles for researching and writing cultural/social histories of mathematics (18th–19th centuries), including choices of scope (case studies vs global survey), structuring periods/themes, and balancing technical detail with accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate mathematical practice within social, political, and technological contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical practice should be analysed as deeply affected by social, political, and technological developments; cultural history is predicated on this assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how changes in society (state formation, industrialisation, communication patterns) prepared the way for institutionalization and professionalization of mathematics; trace links between economic/political needs and mathematical techniques (e.g., surveying, navigation, taxation). Use concrete historical contexts (wars, state reforms) to embed practice in its milieu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider multiple modes of communication (written and oral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study both written forms (journals, correspondence, books) and oral exchanges (lectures, seminars) as central to shaping mathematical communities and knowledge circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the role of scientific journals, the rise of lecture rooms and seminar culture, and letter correspondences (Republic of Letters) when reconstructing how mathematics was produced and disseminated; assess how new communication modes reshaped communities and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case studies when global coverage is impractical and justify selection
rubrics_metrics.description: When a satisfactory global account is impossible, use an illustrative case study (e.g., Victorian Britain) as a lens to explore broader phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the chosen case is representative or informative (e.g., Britain’s global influence in 19th century), and where appropriate, compare and contrast with other regions (e.g., United States) rather than claiming exhaustive global generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on availability, form, and content of education in arithmetic/numeracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate who had access to arithmetic education, what forms it took (memory, rote, reckoning), and which skills textbooks imparted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse textbook content, pedagogy, the social distribution of education, and how curricula treated mechanistic calculation vs reasoning; consider the perceived status of calculation among elites and its place in mass education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine systems of weights, measures, and currency and standardization efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the practical infrastructures (weights, measures, currency) that enabled everyday numerical computation and any efforts to facilitate or standardize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document which systems were in use, reforms (e.g., metric origins), and auxiliary resources available to the public for numerical tasks; link these to changes in numeracy demand (commerce, taxation, surveying).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance analysis of theoretical developments and practical applications (mathesis pura vs applicata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Address both mathematics as pure theory and as applied/tool (mathematical physics, engineering) and their mutual influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace how basic developments (e.g., calculus) enabled applications in mechanics, optics, engineering, and how applied problems in turn spurred new mathematical techniques; treat both strands as essential to the cultural history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure narrative by periods and themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish temporal phases and thematic threads to organise historical analysis (e.g., turn-of-century innovation, mid-century systematisation, late-century disciplinary formation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use periodization to highlight changing intellectual practices (challenge problems, systematisation, foundational debates) and to show transitions (e.g., from practitioners to professional mathematicians); make clear the criteria for chosen period breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive technical jargon; aim for accessible exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Present developments with as little technical language as possible while acknowledging that some formulas/technicalities are unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide non-technical explanations where feasible, reserve technical detail for essential points, and use explanatory scaffolding so readers outside narrow specialties can follow the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse institutional roles and the process of professionalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine institutions (academies, École Polytechnique, observatories, Mint, universities) and their structures (membership categories, pensions, employment) in shaping mathematical careers and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail institutional functions (teaching, consulting, supervising), economic realities (pensions as supplements), and links between state needs and institutional growth; consider how institutions fostered networks and professional identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate interactions between mathematics and wider cultural/philosophical worldviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore how mathematical ideas intersected with philosophical, religious, and literary currents (e.g., Newtonianism, Deism, Romanticism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include philosophical reflections on mathematical truth, the role of mathematics in natural philosophy, and literary/poetic representations; show how worldview debates influenced reception and interpretation of mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate concrete research questions when studying numeracy
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying everyday numeracy, pose targeted questions: extent of education; forms of instruction; skills taught; systems in use; resources available; exposure to numerical data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a checklist for sources and archival work (textbooks, school records, public documents) and to structure empirical chapters; be explicit about geographic and social limits of the evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits and avoid claims of exhaustiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Selectivity is necessary; chapters may highlight important aspects without claiming to exhaust the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about scope, offer retrospection and outlooks where appropriate, and choose representative examples to illuminate tendencies rather than to generalize universally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground claims in historiography and primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Support narrative and interpretations with extensive references to secondary literature and primary documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use and cite relevant scholarship and archival sources (journals, books, government records) to substantiate arguments; include bibliographic apparatus as evidence of engagement with existing literature.
